screens.title: Data Types, Variables, and Operators
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will build a clear mental model of how Solidity represents data and why that model matters for correctness and gas. We start with the core distinction: value types copy data on assignment and function calls, while reference types pass a pointer to the underlying data. That one difference explains a lot of daily errors and gas costs. You will see concrete examples of value types such as unsigned integers, booleans, addresses, fixed-size bytes and enums. Then we move to reference types: arrays, structs and mappings, and how changes through one reference can affect other references. We will also cover the three data locations — storage, memory, and calldata — and when data is persistent on-chain versus transient during a call. Finally, we will review operators you use to compute and compare values, from arithmetic and logical operators to bitwise shifts. By the end you will understand not only the syntax but when to choose storage versus memory versus calldata, and the practical implications for gas and safe updates.

screens.title: Value Types vs Reference Types
screens.narratorSegment: Let's define the two groups you must always keep in mind. Value types include primitive data such as unsigned and signed integers, booleans, addresses, fixed-size bytes, and enums. When you assign or pass a value type, Solidity makes a copy. That means later changes to the original variable will not change the copy — this is predictable and often cheaper. For example, assigning uint a = 5; uint b = a; creates two independent values. By contrast, reference types — arrays, structs and mappings — do not copy the underlying data when assigned. Instead you copy a pointer to the data location. If two variables reference the same storage, a mutation through one reference will be visible through the other. A practical consequence: when you fetch a struct from storage into a local storage reference, updates change the stored state. A common misconception is expecting reference types to behave like value types; this can lead to unintended persistent changes or missed state updates. To check understanding, ask yourself: when I change this variable, do I want a new independent copy, or a shared view of the same data? That question guides whether you choose a value type or reference type.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Value types copy their data; reference types copy a pointer to the data location.

content.html:
Core Concept › Value vs Reference

Definition

Value types hold data directly and copy on assignment. Reference types hold a pointer to data, so assignments copy the reference, not the data.

Value Type Example
uint a = 5; uint b = a; // b is an independent copy
Reference Type Example
uint[] storage arrRef = myArray; // changes through arrRef affect myArray
Common Mistake
Assuming reference assignments create copies and then expecting mutations to be isolated.
Key Takeaway

Pick value types when you need independent data; use reference types when you need shared, mutable state.

Illustrative Scenario
Scenario: Balance Copy
uint a = 100;
uint b = a;
a = 0; // b still 100
Here balance values copy so b remains unchanged after a changes.
Scenario: Array Reference
uint[] storage refArr = products;
refArr.push(5); // products updated
Pushing through the reference mutates the original storage array.

screens.title: Common Value Types: uint, int, bool, address, bytes, enum
screens.narratorSegment: Value types are the simplest building blocks in Solidity. Use uint for non-negative quantities such as token balances or counters; the default uint is uint256. Use int when negative numbers are meaningful, though most financial contracts avoid negative values. A bool is ideal for flags that are true or false. The address type stores 20-byte Ethereum addresses; use address payable when you need to send Ether and convert explicitly with payable(myAddress) when appropriate. Fixed-size bytes, bytes1 through bytes32, are useful for compact storage like hashes or small identifiers; bytes32 is common for storing keccak results. Enums give you a set of named constants, improving clarity and reducing invalid values; for example OrderStatus { Pending, Shipped, Delivered, Cancelled } creates a readable state variable. A frequent misconception is to use strings or bytes for small identifiers instead of bytesN; fixed-size bytes are less gas intensive for short binary data. When picking sizes for uint and int, prefer the default unless you need a smaller footprint. Choosing the right value type improves readability and can reduce gas when used appropriately. Common Value Types: uint, int, bool, address, bytes, enum means select value types to represent quantities, flags, addresses, short binary data, and limited state sets with enums.. In practical terms, when to use each value type and practical examples. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition › Value Types
Integers
uint (unsigned) and int (signed). Defaults are uint256 and int256. Use uint for balances and counters; only use int if negative values are required.
Example: uint256 public balance = 100 ether;
Bool & Address
bool stores true/false flags. address stores 20-byte addresses; address payable can receive Ether and requires explicit payable conversion.
Example: address public ownerAddress; address payable recipient = payable(ownerAddress);
BytesN & Enums
Fixed-size bytes are bytes1..bytes32 for compact binary data. Enums define named constant sets and improve readability and safety.
Example: enum OrderStatus { Pending, Shipped, Delivered, Cancelled }
Practical tip
  • Prefer uint for balances; avoid signed integers unless needed.
  • Use address payable only when sending Ether; cast explicitly.
  • Use bytesN for fixed binary values like hashes to reduce gas.

screens.title: Reference Types: Arrays, Structs, and Mappings
screens.narratorSegment: Reference types group or index data and behave like pointers to an underlying storage location. Arrays can be fixed-size or dynamic. Fixed arrays declare a length and the storage is reserved; dynamic arrays grow and shrink, but resizing and iteration can be gas intensive. Structs let you group related fields—numbers, strings, addresses—into a single composite type, which improves organization and readability. Mappings are key-value stores optimized for efficient lookups; they cannot be iterated and do not expose their keys on-chain. Practical patterns include using an array for ordered collections and a mapping for quick lookups by key. A common mistake is iterating large dynamic arrays on-chain without bounds, which can lead to high gas costs or failed transactions. When storing structs in a storage array, you can create a struct in memory and push it, which avoids accidental persistent mutations until you explicitly write to storage. Remember: when you assign a storage reference to a local variable, updates might modify the stored data immediately. Always choose the right container for the access pattern you need. In practical terms, how solidity stores composite data and when to use each. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition › Reference Types

Arrays

Fixed-size arrays reserve slots; dynamic arrays can grow but may be expensive to resize or iterate.

Code
uint[5] fixedArr;
uint[] public dynamicArr;

Structs & Mappings

Structs group fields; mappings provide efficient key-based access but cannot be iterated when stored on-chain.

Code
struct Person { string name; uint age; address wallet; }
mapping(address => uint) public balances;
Example: Push struct to storage array
Product memory newProduct = Product({
  id: _id,
  name: _name,
  price: _price,
  inStock: true
});
products.push(newProduct);
Create the product in memory to avoid accidental storage mutations, then push to the storage array to persist it.

screens.title: Data Locations: storage, memory, calldata
screens.narratorSegment: Data location is one of the most practical details you will face when designing functions. Storage is where state variables live. Anything stored there is persistent on-chain and therefore more expensive to write and read. Memory exists only during a function call; it is transient and cheaper than storage but still costs gas if large. Calldata is the lightest option for external function parameters: it is read-only and points to the transaction input data. When you declare an external function that accepts a string or array, you must specify calldata for that parameter, and Solidity will avoid copying to memory unless you ask it to. A concrete example: passing a string to an external function as string calldata means you can read it without paying the cost of copying into memory, which reduces gas. A common error is attempting to modify calldata directly — calldata is read-only and cannot be assigned to. Another pitfall is assuming memory modifications persist; they do not. Ask yourself: will this data need to persist after the call? If yes, use storage; if it's read-only input from an external caller, prefer calldata.

keyIdea.title: Data Location Rule
keyIdea.text: Use storage for persistent state, memory for temporary in-call data, calldata for cheap external inputs.

content.html:
Process Flow › storage / memory / calldata
Storage
Persistent state variables live here and remain on-chain between transactions. Writing to storage is expensive.
Example
uint[] public numbers; // stored on-chain
Mistake to avoid
Overwriting large storage structures in a single transaction without considering gas limits.
Memory and Calldata
Memory exists only during calls and is cheaper than storage. Calldata is read-only and cheapest for external inputs because it avoids copies.
Calldata Example
function submit(string calldata s) external { /* read s without copying */ }
Memory Example
function copy(string memory s) internal { /* temporary copy for manipulation */ }
Key Takeaway

Prefer calldata for external read-only inputs, memory for temporary in-call data, storage for persistent state.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough › Example Contract
DataTypesAndOperators (excerpt)
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract DataTypesAndOperators {
    // Value Types
    uint256 public balance = 100 ether; // uint256 is default for uint
    bool public isActive = true;
    address public ownerAddress;
    bytes32 public documentHash; // Fixed-size bytes

    // Enum example
    enum OrderStatus { Pending, Shipped, Delivered, Cancelled }
    OrderStatus public currentStatus = OrderStatus.Pending;

    // Reference Types (storage)
    uint[] public numbers; // Dynamic array of uints
    mapping(address => uint) public balances; // Mapping from address to uint

    struct Product {
        uint id;
        string name;
        uint price;
        bool inStock;
    }
    Product[] public products; // Dynamic array of structs

    constructor(address _owner) {
        ownerAddress = _owner;
        documentHash = keccak256(abi.encodePacked("my_secret_doc")); // Example of bytes32
        balances[_owner] = balance; // Initialize owner's balance in mapping
    }

    function calculateDiscount(uint _price, uint _discountPercent) public pure returns (uint) {
        return _price - (_price * _discountPercent / 100);
    }

    function addProduct(uint _id, string memory _name, uint _price) public {
        Product memory newProduct = Product({
            id: _id,
            name: _name,
            price: _price,
            inStock: true
        });
        products.push(newProduct);
    }

    function updateOrderStatus(OrderStatus newStatus) public {
        currentStatus = newStatus;
    }

    function checkEligibility(uint age, bool hasLicense) public pure returns (bool) {
        return (age >= 18 && hasLicense);
    }
}
Observation
Constructor writes to storage; functions show memory usage and pure computations.
Example
addProduct creates a Product in memory and then pushes to storage.
Takeaway
Split pure logic and state changes for clarity and cheaper testing.

screens.title: Operators: Arithmetic, Comparison, Logical, and Bitwise
screens.narratorSegment: Operators let you compute results and make decisions. Solidity provides arithmetic operators like addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, modulo and exponentiation. Always be cautious of division by zero when writing code that divides. Comparison operators return boolean values and include equality and inequality and the relational operators less-than and greater-than. Logical operators combine boolean expressions with AND, OR, and NOT. Bitwise operators operate on integer bits and include bitwise AND, OR, XOR, NOT, and left and right shifts. They are powerful for compact state representations but can be confusing if you are not thinking in terms of bits. Assignment and compound assignment operators such as plus-equals are available, and increment/decrement operators exist too. A concrete example from the contract is calculateDiscount which composes multiplication and division to avoid floating-point arithmetic; it uses integer math to compute a percent reduction. A common misconception is to expect floating-point semantics; Solidity uses integer math, so structure your calculations to avoid truncation or precision loss. End with this check: when you perform a calculation, have you considered integer division, division by zero, and whether bitwise logic matches your intent?

Core Concept › Operators
Arithmetic & Comparison
// Arithmetic
+  -  *  /  %  **

// Comparison
==  !=  <  <=  >  >=
Remember integer division truncates; plan expressions to minimize precision loss.
Logical & Bitwise
// Logical
&&  ||  !

// Bitwise
&  |  ^  ~  <<  >>
Use bitwise ops when you need compact flags or shifts. Keep code readable and documented.

screens.title: Arrays in Practice: Fixed vs Dynamic and Gas Considerations
screens.narratorSegment: Arrays are useful collections but they come with trade-offs. A fixed-size array declares a compile-time length and reserves slots; it can be slightly more predictable for gas. Dynamic arrays allow push and pop but growing them and iterating through large arrays can be expensive. When designing functions that operate on arrays, consider whether you need to process entire arrays on-chain. Iterating unboundedly over a large dynamic array can cause transactions to run out of gas. Instead, prefer indexed access, mappings for lookup, or off-chain indexing for heavy processing. Another useful pattern is to keep array sizes small and limit on-chain loops. Concrete example: a dynamic uint[] public numbers can be appended to safely, but avoid a function that loops through the whole numbers array to perform heavy computation. Common misconception: thinking dynamic arrays are cheap to iterate — they are not. For tasks like summarizing large datasets, consider reading events or using off-chain tooling. Always ask: can I restructure my data or logic to avoid long on-chain loops? screens.title: Common Mistakes, Pitfalls, and Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize common pitfalls and best practices so you avoid them in real contracts. First, do not assume reference types behave like value types; assignment can create shared references that modify storage. Second, never try to modify calldata — it is read-only. If you need a writable copy, declare a memory variable and copy explicitly. Third, avoid unbounded on-chain iteration; large loops can fail or be costly. Prefer mappings for lookups and move heavy aggregation off-chain. Fourth, be explicit about data locations for reference type parameters; external functions must use calldata. Fifth, use memory when constructing temporary structs before pushing to storage to avoid accidental persistent mutations. Sixth, watch arithmetic: Solidity uses integer arithmetic, not floating point, so plan expressions to avoid truncation and check division by zero scenarios. A useful best practice: split pure computations from state changes — mark functions pure when they do not touch storage and use view when they only read. These habits improve safety, predictability, and gas efficiency. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will build a clear mental model of how Solidity represents data and why that model matters for correctness and gas. We start with the core distinction: value types copy data on assignment and function calls, while reference types pass a pointer to the underlying data. That one difference explains a lot of daily errors and gas costs. You will see concrete examples of value types such as unsigned integers, booleans, addresses, fixed-size bytes and enums. Then we move to reference types: arrays, structs and mappings, and how changes through one reference can affect other references. We will also cover the three data locations — storage, memory, and calldata — and when data is persistent on-chain versus transient during a call. Finally, we will review operators you use to compute and compare values, from arithmetic and logical operators to bitwise shifts. By the end you will understand not only the syntax but when to choose storage versus memory versus calldata, and the practical implications for gas and safe updates.

By the end of this chapter you will distinguish value types from reference types and know why that matters for copying, mutation, and gas. You will master common value types such as unsigned and signed integers, booleans, addresses, fixed-size bytes, and enums so you can pick the right type for balances, flags, and identifiers. You will understand reference types—arrays, structs, mappings—and how their pointer-like behavior affects updates and visibility across function calls. Finally, you will be able to explain storage, memory, and calldata and choose the correct data location for function parameters to avoid costly or incorrect behavior. Each objective pairs a clear skill with a practical why: correctness, gas efficiency, and safer contract design. We will practice these with concrete code examples and a guided product catalog activity to reinforce learning.

This second objectives view focuses on measurable practice outcomes you will verify in code. You will implement and inspect state variables in storage and confirm that modifying a referenced struct affects stored state. You will write functions that accept array and string parameters with explicit memory or calldata locations and observe gas differences when you avoid unnecessary copies. You will design a product catalog using a struct and a mapping, and construct add and toggle functions so you can validate behavior with get functions. Lastly, you will write small pure functions that use arithmetic, comparison, logical, and bitwise operators and identify where division by zero or incorrect bit operations could cause errors. These are the capabilities you will demonstrate during exercises and the hands-on activity included in the chapter. Learning Objectives — Practice & Assessment means implement the contract patterns and verify changes that prove understanding of mutability and data locations.. In practical terms, skills to verify with code and tests. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's define the two groups you must always keep in mind. Value types include primitive data such as unsigned and signed integers, booleans, addresses, fixed-size bytes, and enums. When you assign or pass a value type, Solidity makes a copy. That means later changes to the original variable will not change the copy — this is predictable and often cheaper. For example, assigning uint a = 5; uint b = a; creates two independent values. By contrast, reference types — arrays, structs and mappings — do not copy the underlying data when assigned. Instead you copy a pointer to the data location. If two variables reference the same storage, a mutation through one reference will be visible through the other. A practical consequence: when you fetch a struct from storage into a local storage reference, updates change the stored state. A common misconception is expecting reference types to behave like value types; this can lead to unintended persistent changes or missed state updates. To check understanding, ask yourself: when I change this variable, do I want a new independent copy, or a shared view of the same data? That question guides whether you choose a value type or reference type.

Value types are the simplest building blocks in Solidity. Use uint for non-negative quantities such as token balances or counters; the default uint is uint256. Use int when negative numbers are meaningful, though most financial contracts avoid negative values. A bool is ideal for flags that are true or false. The address type stores 20-byte Ethereum addresses; use address payable when you need to send Ether and convert explicitly with payable(myAddress) when appropriate. Fixed-size bytes, bytes1 through bytes32, are useful for compact storage like hashes or small identifiers; bytes32 is common for storing keccak results. Enums give you a set of named constants, improving clarity and reducing invalid values; for example OrderStatus { Pending, Shipped, Delivered, Cancelled } creates a readable state variable. A frequent misconception is to use strings or bytes for small identifiers instead of bytesN; fixed-size bytes are less gas intensive for short binary data. When picking sizes for uint and int, prefer the default unless you need a smaller footprint. Choosing the right value type improves readability and can reduce gas when used appropriately. Common Value Types: uint, int, bool, address, bytes, enum means select value types to represent quantities, flags, addresses, short binary data, and limited state sets with enums.. In practical terms, when to use each value type and practical examples. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Reference types group or index data and behave like pointers to an underlying storage location. Arrays can be fixed-size or dynamic. Fixed arrays declare a length and the storage is reserved; dynamic arrays grow and shrink, but resizing and iteration can be gas intensive. Structs let you group related fields—numbers, strings, addresses—into a single composite type, which improves organization and readability. Mappings are key-value stores optimized for efficient lookups; they cannot be iterated and do not expose their keys on-chain. Practical patterns include using an array for ordered collections and a mapping for quick lookups by key. A common mistake is iterating large dynamic arrays on-chain without bounds, which can lead to high gas costs or failed transactions. When storing structs in a storage array, you can create a struct in memory and push it, which avoids accidental persistent mutations until you explicitly write to storage. Remember: when you assign a storage reference to a local variable, updates might modify the stored data immediately. Always choose the right container for the access pattern you need. Reference Types: Arrays, Structs, and Mappings means use arrays for ordered data, structs for grouped fields, and mappings for fast key-value lookups; be mindful of iteration costs.. In practical terms, how solidity stores composite data and when to use each. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Data location is one of the most practical details you will face when designing functions. Storage is where state variables live. Anything stored there is persistent on-chain and therefore more expensive to write and read. Memory exists only during a function call; it is transient and cheaper than storage but still costs gas if large. Calldata is the lightest option for external function parameters: it is read-only and points to the transaction input data. When you declare an external function that accepts a string or array, you must specify calldata for that parameter, and Solidity will avoid copying to memory unless you ask it to. A concrete example: passing a string to an external function as string calldata means you can read it without paying the cost of copying into memory, which reduces gas. A common error is attempting to modify calldata directly — calldata is read-only and cannot be assigned to. Another pitfall is assuming memory modifications persist; they do not. Ask yourself: will this data need to persist after the call? If yes, use storage; if it's read-only input from an external caller, prefer calldata.

Operators let you compute results and make decisions. Solidity provides arithmetic operators like addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, modulo and exponentiation. Always be cautious of division by zero when writing code that divides. Comparison operators return boolean values and include equality and inequality and the relational operators less-than and greater-than. Logical operators combine boolean expressions with AND, OR, and NOT. Bitwise operators operate on integer bits and include bitwise AND, OR, XOR, NOT, and left and right shifts. They are powerful for compact state representations but can be confusing if you are not thinking in terms of bits. Assignment and compound assignment operators such as plus-equals are available, and increment/decrement operators exist too. Let's summarize common pitfalls and best practices so you avoid them in real contracts. First, do not assume reference types behave like value types; assignment can create shared references that modify storage. Second, never try to modify calldata — it is read-only. If you need a writable copy, declare a memory variable and copy explicitly. Third, avoid unbounded on-chain iteration; large loops can fail or be costly. Prefer mappings for lookups and move heavy aggregation off-chain. Fourth, be explicit about data locations for reference type parameters; external functions must use calldata. Fifth, use memory when constructing temporary structs before pushing to storage to avoid accidental persistent mutations. Sixth, watch arithmetic: Solidity uses integer arithmetic, not floating point, so plan expressions to avoid truncation and check division by zero scenarios. A useful best practice: split pure computations from state changes — mark functions pure when they do not touch storage and use view when they only read. These habits improve safety, predictability, and gas efficiency. Let's close by rehearsing the essential concepts you should keep at hand. Value types copy values on assignment; they are simple and predictably isolated. Reference types like arrays, structs, and mappings pass references that point to underlying data and can lead to shared mutations. Storage is persistent on-chain and expensive to write to; memory is temporary for function execution; calldata is the cheapest read-only location for external inputs. Choose the right combination of types and locations to balance correctness and gas costs. Operators let you compute and compare values; remember Solidity uses integer arithmetic and offers bitwise operations for compact bit-level logic.
